name: Cyclic glycine-proline (cGP)

lead: Cyclic glycine-proline is a small peptide the body makes from IGF-1 and that is also found in foods like blackcurrant.
People take it as a supplement for IGF-1 regulation and healthy aging.

paras: It binds IGFBP-3, which changes how much IGF-1 is freely available.
Human data are limited to small studies; reported research is mostly in animals.

angle.text: Users take it hoping to support IGF-1 function with age, which they associate with overall vitality and a younger-looking state.

lead: Cyclic glycine-proline (cGP) is a small cyclic dipeptide that the body forms as a metabolite of IGF-1, and that also occurs in some foods and marine organisms [1][2]. It is sold as a supplement by people interested in healthy-aging and IGF-1 function.

cGP binds IGF binding protein-3 and so influences how much IGF-1 is available in circulation [3][4]. Its link to appearance is indirect: people discuss it for longevity, IGF-1 balance and general healthy aging.

paras: cGP retains affinity for IGFBP-3 and competes with IGF-1 for binding, which regulates bioavailable IGF-1; the cGP/IGF-1 molar ratio has been proposed as a measure of functional IGF-1 [3][4].

Reviews describe neuroprotective effects of IGF-1 derived peptides in animal models [5]. In obese rats, cGP lowered systolic blood pressure and retroperitoneal fat weight [6]. In a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease it improved memory and reduced plaque load [7]. Observational work found that stroke patients with higher plasma cGP/IGF-1 ratios had better outcomes [8].

A trial in 11 Parkinson patients found blackcurrant anthocyanin supplementation for 28 days raised cerebrospinal fluid cGP; cGP was present in the supplement [2]. Patient studies of the cGP/IGF-1 ratio are observational [3][8]. No trials of cGP as a stand-alone supplement for appearance were found.
